name: Sinte-Manus Romani
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file
sweep_summary: Sinte-Manus Romani (sint1235) is not in the catalog. Both sweep items are Glottolog machine misassignments (the reference records say 'computerized assignment from "mesto"' / '"wesen"'): Diesing & Zec 2016 is about Serbian enclitic placement and Peco 1976 about Serbo-Croatian pitch accent - neither concerns Romani; priority none, not fetched sources. The sweep did locate and read a first-hand open source: Finck 1903, Lehrbuch des Dialekts der deutschen Zigeuner (archive.org, saved with page images checked), whose §§ 3-7 (pp. 4-7) give a full word-stress description for German Sinti: initial stress in nominative nouns and uninflected words, stress on the syllable before Layer-II case/vocative suffixes, theme-vowel stress in the present and final (person-suffix) stress in the preterite, German loans keeping German stress, plus lexical exceptions. Matras 2006 (ELL, open PDF via Wayback) gives the pan-Romani frame: conservative final stress with leftward shift in western/central European dialects. The modern full grammar Holzinger 1993 has no online copy (Harvard print only) and is the high-priority acquisition.

earlier_scan.source_named: Holzinger, Daniel (1993). Das Romanes: Grammatik und Diskursanalyse der Sprache der Sinte. Innsbruck. (full grammar of Sinte Romani; no online copy located)

new_statements.quote: § 5. In den § 4 nicht angeführten Kasusformen, nämlich im Nominativ, Objektiv sowie den Vokativformen ohne -ja, -je, -le, wird, von den § 6 erwähnten Ausnahmen abgesehn, die erste Silbe am stärksten hervorgehoben, z. B. o báro rai 'der Richter' […], máro 'Brot', štíləpen 'Gefängnis' u. s. w. § 6. Eine Ausnahme von der § 5 aufgestellten Regel bilden: a) alle Nomina mit dem Suffix -kəro, -kəri […], bei denen die dem Suffix unmittelbar vorausgehende Silbe am stärksten hervorgehoben wird […]; b) alle Nomina mit langem Vokal in vorletzter Silbe, bei denen diese am stärksten hervorgehoben wird, z. B. lowína 'Bier', sapúni 'Seife' […] § 7. Bei den nicht flektierbaren Wörtern wird meistens die erste Silbe am stärksten hervorgehoben.
new_statements.translation: § 5. In the case forms not listed in § 4, namely in the nominative, objective, and the vocative forms without -ja, -je, -le, the first syllable is most strongly prominent, apart from the exceptions mentioned in § 6, e.g. o báro rai 'the judge' […], máro 'bread', štíləpen 'prison', etc. § 6. Exceptions to the rule set up in § 5 are: a) all nouns with the suffix -kəro, -kəri […], in which the syllable immediately preceding the suffix is most strongly prominent […]; b) all nouns with a long vowel in the penultimate syllable, in which that syllable is most strongly prominent, e.g. lowína 'beer', sapúni 'soap' […] § 7. In the uninflected words the first syllable is mostly the most strongly prominent.
new_statements.citation: Finck, Franz Nikolaus (1903). Lehrbuch des Dialekts der deutschen Zigeuner. Marburg: N. G. Elwert.
new_statements.locator: Zweites Kapitel 'Das Lautgefüge', A. Stärkeabstufung, I. Innerhalb des einzelnen Worts, §§ 3, 5, 6, 7, pp. 4–7 (PDF pp. 26–29); quote from § 5 (p. 5), § 6 a–b (p. 5) and § 7 (p. 7)
new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation/base forms (nominative and objective of nouns, bare vocatives, imperatives, ā-stem present forms, most indeclinables) stress is on the first (root) syllable; stress moves to the syllable immediately before Layer-II case suffixes (-ke, -te, -tər, -sa) and vocative -ja/-je/-le, to the theme vowel before personal endings in consonant/e-stem presents, and to the final person suffix in the preterite (hund-óm). A long penult attracts stress (lowína); -kəro/-kəri derivatives stress the pre-suffix syllable; German loans keep their German stress. So the position is fixed by morphological category, with a root-initial default and a weight-sensitive exception.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Finck does not discuss secondary stress. von Sowa 1888 (East Prussian sub-dialect, p. 91) notes that trisyllabic words 'haben meist einen starken Nebenton auf der Anlautsilbe'.
new_statements.exceptions: § 6 a–f: -kəro/-kəri derivatives (pre-suffix), long-penult nouns (penult), nouns in -itsa/-itska (first syllable of the suffix), bi-/tsi- negatives (keep base stress; a–c override), deš- numeral compounds (first syllable of second element), and a long list of individually non-initial nouns/pronouns (amáro, brišíndo, rašái, sonəkái, tumé …); § 7 lists final-stressed adverbs/prepositions (adrín, akána, aprál, durál, palál, telál …); § 3 Anm. 1: German verbs with Romani suffix keep German stress; Anm. 3: imperfect/pluperfect stress the syllable before -es, so the copula is always initially stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Innerhalb des einzelnen Worts', §§ 2–7); § 8 says sentence-level prominence follows German except that a pronoun after a preposition is always stressed. Describes the (western) German Sinti dialect of Finck's informants; von Sowa's 1888/1889/1893 articles show sub-dialectal variation (East Prussian: final stress the rule; Westphalian: never beyond antepenult, long penult stressed; Bohemian: penult as a rule).
new_statements.identity_note: Finck 1903 describes the dialect of the 'deutsche Zigeuner' = German Sinti, i.e. Sinte Romani proper (sint1235; the Glottolog language-level entry, no separate dialect code). von Sowa's 1888/1889/1893 articles (also saved) describe three named sub-dialects of the same German Sinti — East Prussian (final stress the rule), Westphalian (stress within the last three syllables, long penult stressed) and NW-Bohemian (penult the rule) — showing that the stress position varies across Sinti sub-dialects and is not stable across the cluster; the Italian (Piedmontese/Lombard) and French Manuš varieties were not covered by any opened source.

new_statements.quote: § 4. In den mit einem der Suffixe -ja, -je, -le gebildeten Vokativformen (§ 37 b) sowie den aus dem Obliquus durch eins der Suffixe -ke, -te, -tər, -sa [...] gebildeten Kasusformen (§ 38) ist die dem Suffix unmittelbar vorausgehende Silbe die stärkst betonte [...]. § 5. In den § 4 nicht angeführten Kasusformen, nämlich im Nominativ, Objektiv sowie den Vokativformen ohne -ja, -je, -le, wird, von den § 6 erwähnten Ausnahmen abgesehn, die erste Silbe am stärksten hervorgehoben, z. B. o báro rai 'der Richter' [...], mála 'Kamerad, Freund!', máro 'Brot', štíləpen 'Gefängnis' u. s. w.
new_statements.translation: § 4. In the vocative forms built with one of the suffixes -ja, -je, -le (§ 37b) and in the case forms built from the oblique with one of the suffixes -ke, -te, -tər, -sa [...] (§ 38), the syllable immediately preceding the suffix is the most strongly stressed [...]. § 5. In the case forms not listed in § 4, namely the nominative, objective, and the vocative forms without -ja, -je, -le, apart from the exceptions mentioned in § 6, the first syllable is most strongly prominent, e.g. o báro rai 'the judge' [...], mála 'comrade, friend!', máro 'bread', štíləpen 'prison', etc.
new_statements.citation: Finck, Franz Nikolaus (1903). Lehrbuch des Dialekts der deutschen Zigeuner. Marburg: N. G. Elwert.
new_statements.locator: Zweites Kapitel, A. Stärkeabstufung, § 4-5, p. 5 (PDF p. 27); verbs § 3, p. 4; exceptions § 6, pp. 5-6; uninflected words § 7, p. 7
new_statements.reading: German Sinti (Sinte Romani) as described by Finck in 1903 has morphologically conditioned stress: the citation/nominative form of nouns and most uninflected words carry INITIAL stress (a German-style shift away from the conservative Romani final stress noted by Matras 2006), while Layer-II case forms and -ja/-je/-le vocatives stress the syllable right before the suffix (i.e. the oblique-stem final), present-tense verbs stress the theme vowel before the person ending, and preterites stress the final person suffix; German loan verbs keep German stress. There are listed lexical exceptions (nouns in -kəro, long penults, -itsa, and a word list such as amáro, rašái, sonakái). For catalog purposes: not a fixed-position system; initial-stress default in citation forms with morphological (suffix-preceding / final) stress in inflected forms and lexical exceptions.

sources.note: Detailed word-stress rules: imperative and ā-stem present stress the first (root) syllable; consonant/e-stem present stresses the syllable before the personal ending (theme vowel); preterite stresses the final syllable (person suffix); nominative/objective and bare vocatives stress the first syllable; vocatives in -ja/-je/-le and Layer-II case forms (-ke, -te, -tər, -sa) stress the syllable before the suffix; exceptions: -kəro/-kəri derivatives (pre-suffix), nouns with long penult (penult), -itsa/-itska nouns, bi-/tsi- negatives, deš- compounds, and a list of individual lexemes; indeclinables…

sources.note: For the Bohemian (B., NW Bohemia) sub-dialect: 'In B. liegt der Accent in der Regel auf der vorletzten Silbe'; a penult with a reduced vowel is skipped (antepenult stressed); some words and all consonant-final perfect forms stress the final syllable; case suffixes sometimes draw stress to the penult, sometimes not; refers to ZVPS for the East-Prussian and Westphalian sub-dialects.

sources.citation: von Sowa, Rudolf (1889). Die Mundart der westfälischen Zigeuner. Zeitschrift für Völkerpsychologie und Sprachwissenschaft 19: 193 ff. ('III. Betonung', pp. 200–201).
sources.note: Westphalian German Sinti: stress never goes further back than the antepenult; -engero/-engəri formations and -alo adjectives stress the antepenult (the latter also with a strong final accent that often becomes main stress); words with a long penult usually stress it (present forms kuráva, kuréla, kuréna); a closed penult does not necessarily carry main stress; -in/-li nouns often final; subjunctive present final.

sources.citation: von Sowa, Rudolf (1888). Die Mundart der ostpreussischen Zigeuner. Zeitschrift für Völkerpsychologie und Sprachwissenschaft 18: 82–93 (stress pp. 90–91).
sources.note: East Prussian German Sinti: 'die Betonung der Endsilbe [ist] in dieser Mundart Regel', with strong wavering and real exceptions; German loans keep stem stress; a closed or long penult is often stressed; trisyllables carry a strong secondary stress on the first syllable; case suffixes unstressed (except locative -e); 1/3 sg. and 2/3 pl. present stress the penult; perfect forms waver.
